title: Hexadecimal, shifts & masks
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which type stores whether a sensor is active?
Choose −18 in sign magnitude, then two’s complement.
questions.feedback: Start +18 = 00010010; set sign or invert and add 1.

questions.prompt: Add signed 01110000 and 00100000. Which is correct?

blocks.title: Convert using nibbles
blocks.text: Hexadecimal is base 16: A–F represent 10–15. One hex digit represents four bits. 173 ÷ 16 = 10 remainder 13, so 173 = AD = 1010 1101 in binary. Hex is shorter to read; it does not reduce stored bits.

blocks.title: Logical shifts
blocks.text: Fill vacated positions with zeros and discard bits leaving the fixed width. Left k places multiplies an unsigned value by 2ᵏ only if no significant bits are lost. Right k places divides by 2ᵏ and discards the remainder. 45 >> 2 gives 11.

blocks.title: Masks
blocks.text: AND: 1 preserves, 0 clears. OR: 1 sets, 0 preserves. XOR: 1 toggles, 0 preserves. Number bits 7 to 0 from left to right. 10100101 AND 00001111 = 00000101.

questions.prompt: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent?

questions.feedback: A mask bit of 1 flips the corresponding bit.

blocks.title: Use the method
blocks.text: Refer to the worked explanation above. Work out each answer before checking the feedback.

questions.feedback: Zeros enter on the left; result is 13.
Keep the low nibble and clear the high nibble.

questions.prompt: Logically shift 10100001 one place left in eight bits.
questions.feedback: The leftmost 1 is discarded; stored value is 66.

questions.prompt: Choose an operation and mask to set bits 3 and 0, preserving all others.
questions.feedback: OR guarantees the selected bits become 1.

questions.prompt: Choose an operation and mask to clear bits 7 and 6, preserving all others.
questions.feedback: Mask zeros clear the two high bits; ones preserve the rest.

writing.prompt: Explain why an eight-bit logical left shift of 10100001 does not double its stored unsigned value. Give the original value, stored result and general condition for doubling.
writing.model: 10100001 represents 161. A one-place left shift gives stored byte 01000010, representing 66. The leading 1 is discarded because only eight bits are retained; 322 cannot fit. A logical left shift doubles an unsigned value only when no significant bit is lost.

questions.prompt: Hexadecimal reduces the number of bits needed to store the same value.
questions.feedback: It shortens the written representation only.

questions.prompt: A logical right shift inserts zeros on the left.
questions.feedback: This is a logical shift, not sign extension.

questions.prompt: XOR with a mask bit of 1 always sets the data bit to 1.
